Editor's Note: Xie Maosong is a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies at Tsinghua University. This article reflects the author's opinions and not necessarily the views of CGTN.
As a political party that has been in power for decades, the Communist Party of China (CPC) recognizes that it faces enduring challenges in maintaining its governing capacity and staying connected with the public. These include the tests of governance, reform and opening up, the market economy and the external environment, as well as the risks of complacency, inadequate governing capacity, detachment from the people and corruption. Pointless formality, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance pose additional challenges to effective governance.
For the CPC, addressing these challenges requires strengthening Party building, advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, and promoting self-reform. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, these efforts have been pursued as a sustained, comprehensive undertaking, with full and rigorous Party self-governance integrated into every aspect of Party building.
A sculpture of the Communist Party of China flag at the Museum of the Communist Party of China in Beijing, China. 
Improving work styles and enforcing discipline
The CPC regards the conduct of a governing party as a matter directly related to its long-term viability. The Eight-Point Decision on Improving Party and Government Conduct, introduced in 2012, has been a landmark measure in advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance.
Spelled out in just over 600 words, the eight-point rules target pointless formality, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, while opposing privilege and misconduct. According to the rules, when conducting grassroots field studies, officials should learn from the people on the ground. Ceremonial formalities such as banners and floral arrangements are not allowed. Official meetings and events must be streamlined. Security protocols such as traffic controls and road or venue closures should be minimized.
The CPC has stressed leading by example, with senior officials setting the standards for the wider Party. Behind seemingly individual problems such as wasteful spending and detachment from the public, the Party also seeks to address deeper risks involving the abuse of power for private gain and the improper handling of private and public interests.
The CPC considers the experience of advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance through improvements in work style an important lesson in its broader efforts at self-reform.
Discipline is another key pillar. The CPC maintains that Party discipline must be stricter than the requirements of national law, covering political conduct, organizational responsibilities, integrity, relations with the public and personal behavior. While the law sets the minimum standard for lawful conduct, Party rules impose additional obligations on members and officials. The aim is to identify and address misconduct at an early stage, before minor violations develop into more serious problems.
An official from local market regulation authorities tells local residents how to identify counterfeit goods in Taizhou City, east China's Zhejiang Province, March 9, 2026. 
Sustaining the fight against corruption
The CPC regards corruption as a major threat to its governing foundation and considers combating it a long-term task that requires both determination and institutional safeguards.
Since 2012, the Party has pursued an extensive anti-corruption campaign targeting high-ranking officials, misconduct at the grassroots level and corruption involving officials who have fled overseas. It has paid particular attention to sectors where power, public funds and resources are concentrated, as well as improper ties between officials and business interests.
Following the 20th CPC National Congress in late 2022, China's disciplinary agencies have handled 768,000 cases of malpractice and corruption at the grassroots level, imposing penalties on 628,000 officials, according to the National Commission of Supervision.
The CPC also emphasizes preventing the use of political power to protect capital and the penetration of capital into the political sphere. It requires leading officials to exercise strict oversight over the conduct of their spouses, children and other close relatives.
The Party maintains that it does not represent the interests of any particular interest group, and presents its anti-corruption efforts as part of a broader effort to safeguard the public interest.
A central principle of this approach is to address corruption through three interconnected measures: making officials afraid to engage in corruption, making it impossible for them to do so, and fostering an unwillingness to do so.
The first relies on strict enforcement and credible deterrence. The second focuses on improving institutions, tightening oversight and placing checks on the exercise of power. The third emphasizes education, ethical awareness and a stronger commitment to public service.
These measures are intended to reinforce one another: enforcement deters misconduct, institutions reduce opportunities for abuse, and ethical education seeks to strengthen officials' commitment to integrity.
Members of the Communist Party of China renew the Party admission oath in Qujing, southwest China's Yunnan Province, June 26, 2026. 
Constraining power through institutions
The CPC emphasizes that combating corruption requires more than investigating individual cases. It also requires effective systems to regulate how power is exercised.
This involves strengthening internal Party regulations, clarifying the responsibilities and limits of officials, standardizing administrative procedures and improving oversight of key powers, including policymaking, administrative approvals, regulation and law enforcement.
The Party also seeks to integrate different forms of supervision, including routine oversight by Party organizations, disciplinary inspection, supervisory authorities, audits, inspections and public reporting. Together, these mechanisms are intended to strengthen accountability throughout the exercise of power and reduce opportunities for misconduct.
Organizational discipline and personnel management are also important parts of this framework. The CPC emphasizes selecting and appointing officials according to appropriate standards, promoting a sound understanding of governance performance and addressing improper practices in personnel decisions.
Institutional development underpins these efforts. By incorporating Party governance into a more comprehensive system of internal rules and regulations, the CPC seeks to make discipline and accountability an enduring part of its governance rather than relying solely on periodic campaigns.
Ultimately, the CPC presents full and rigorous Party self-governance as a means of strengthening its long-term governing capacity. Its approach combines improvements in work style, strict discipline, anti-corruption efforts, institutional oversight and organizational reform, with the stated goal of ensuring that officials exercise power responsibly and remain committed to serving the people.
For political parties seeking to sustain their governing capacity over the long term, the CPC's experience highlights the importance of continuous self-reform, effective internal rules, accountability and a sustained commitment to public service.

articles.fullText:
The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital of Yerevan has entered its final stretch.
The conference has adopted 14 decisions and secured more than $1.8 billion in financial commitments. Yet negotiators remain divided over some of the most contentious issues, including who should bear the cost of protecting nature and how global commitments can be translated into measurable results.
With the conference due to conclude on Friday, the focus has shifted from reaffirming global biodiversity goals to reaching agreement on how to achieve them.
Participants attend the COP 17 to the CBD in Yerevan, Armenia, October 27, 2026. 
Tangible progress
The COP17 marks the first global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022 with 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
There are encouraging signs of international cooperation, said Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, noting that nearly 90% of the convention's parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than 70% have submitted national reports.
The negotiations have also yielded concrete results. Parties have adopted 14 decisions under the convention, covering areas such as invasive alien species, biosafety, gender equality and education.
Funding announcements have added to the summit's momentum, with new commitments from governments, philanthropic organizations and other partners.
The Executive Council of the China-initiated Kunming Biodiversity Fund has approved nine biodiversity conservation projects worth roughly $4.5 million for developing nations, Dong Baotong, vice minister of China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment, said Monday.
China has contributed 400 million yuan (about $60 million) to the fund, which supports biodiversity conservation in developing countries. Schomaker depicted the initiative as an agile instrument for channeling support to where it is needed.
Elsewhere, nine philanthropic organizations pledged $500 million through 2030 for species recovery, while the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund secured over $60 million in new pledges.
These achievements demonstrate that environmental multilateralism is continuing to deliver, even amid profound geopolitical shifts, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
"Nature is not a luxury we protect when economies can afford it," said Andersen. "Nature is what makes economies possible."
An installation sits outside the venue during the COP 17 to the CBD in Yerevan, Armenia, October 27, 2026. 
Obstacles ahead
Securing new financial commitments is one thing; establishing a sustainable, long-term funding model for biodiversity conservation is another.
Despite the pledges announced in Yerevan, countries remain divided over who should contribute to international biodiversity finance, how much they should pay and how the funds should be allocated.
Other sticking points include reforming subsidies and incentives that harm nature, arrangements for indigenous peoples and local communities, and aligning biodiversity action with climate commitments and other international obligations.
Andersen said ministers are attending the conference's final week to help break the deadlock, particularly on resource mobilization and the global review.
"Financing the destruction of nature with 30 dollars against every dollar spent restoring it is like paying 30 people to tear down your house for every one hired to rebuild it," Schomaker said, framing the way forward around three priorities: accountability, alignment and acceleration.
According to Schomaker, "accountability" means identifying where countries are falling short through national reporting and scientific evidence, while "acceleration" means stepping up efforts to meet the framework's 2030 targets. "Alignment" may prove the hardest part, requiring governments to ensure that public budgets, private investment, economic policies and financial incentives reinforce rather than undermine biodiversity objectives.
The private sector is already pressing for change. More than 130 businesses and financial institutions have called for faster reform of incentives harmful to biodiversity.
Yet, for companies and investors, uncertainty remains over how global biodiversity targets will translate into national regulations, investment requirements and standards for measuring conservation results. Without clearer and more consistent rules, even a growing willingness to invest in nature may struggle to produce results at scale.
Meanwhile, the environmental pressures driving the negotiations are intensifying. UNEP's latest Emissions Gap Report warns that global warming could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius this century under current policies, with potentially severe consequences for ecosystems and biodiversity.
The United Nations' State of Biodiversity Action report, released ahead of COP17, found that fewer than half of the national biodiversity targets assessed by countries were on track.
Against this backdrop, much now hinges on the proposed "Yerevan Pathway," a document that identifies measurable priorities to address gaps in implementing global biodiversity targets over the next two years.
The conference has already shown that multilateral cooperation can deliver decisions and mobilize resources. Whether it can also resolve the harder questions of financing and implementation will be the real test of its success.
"COP17 will be judged by the long-term results we achieve together after the conference, rather than the number of statements made in Yerevan," said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.

China's experience in biodiversity conservation offers valuable lessons for the world, particularly in combining ambitious commitments with sound science, effective institutions and long-term investment, the UN biodiversity chief said on Monday.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), made the remarks on the sidelines of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the CBD (COP17), which began on Monday in Yerevan, capital of Armenia.
A Yunnan snub-nosed monkey, Yunnan Province, southwest China. 
China's experience is particularly evident in the scale of its conservation efforts and its integration of biodiversity into national development planning, Schomaker said.
Its ecological conservation redline system, national parks network, ecological restoration programs and investments in biodiversity monitoring demonstrate practical approaches to implementing national commitments, she said.
In her eyes, three lessons stand out from China's experience: conservation must be integrated into broader economic and land-use planning; ecological restoration requires sustained investment; and effective monitoring is essential to measuring results.
China's contribution extends beyond its domestic efforts. "Its continued support for multilateral cooperation is especially valuable amid today's geopolitical challenges," Schomaker said.
Schomaker highlighted China's role in securing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), one of the most significant international agreements for nature in decades.
Smart drip irrigation waters forage grass in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, north China, June 12, 2026. 
As COP15 president, China helped guide complex negotiations among countries with different priorities and capacities. Working closely with Canada, host of the Montreal meeting, China helped build the consensus needed to adopt the framework and its 23 targets, she said.
"That was a landmark diplomatic achievement," Schomaker said. Four years later, the challenge is to turn the agreement into measurable results. "COP15 gave us the plan. COP17 is about making that plan work."
Financing is key to implementation. China established the Kunming Biodiversity Fund to help developing countries strengthen their capacity for biodiversity conservation. Schomaker described the fund as an important instrument for the CBD, created specifically to support implementation of the KMGBF.
She also highlighted the fund's ability to attract private-sector contributions alongside China's government funding.
Schomaker deems South-South cooperation particularly valuable because countries facing similar challenges can share practical experience, technology and expertise.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, addresses a press conference in Yerevan, Armenia, October 15, 2026. 
The first global review of progress in implementing the KMGBF, to be conducted at COP17, shows encouraging engagement, Schomaker said. Nearly 90% of parties have established national biodiversity targets, and more than 140 countries have submitted national reports. However, fewer than half of the aligned national targets assessed by parties themselves are currently on track.
The largest gaps concern targets requiring changes to economic systems, particularly those related to business impacts and disclosure, sustainable consumption, harmful subsidies and biodiversity finance. Significant shortfalls also remain in protected-area coverage and efforts to address invasive alien species, she said.
"The fundamental challenge is that biodiversity cannot remain the responsibility of environment ministries alone." Progress increasingly depends on decisions by finance, agriculture, energy and other economic ministries, Schomaker said.
A major challenge is ensuring that developing countries have adequate, predictable and accessible financial resources to implement their commitments, she said. Developing countries emphasize the need for greater international support, while developed countries stress mobilizing finance from a wider range of sources and improving its effectiveness. Both are essential.
Countries have agreed to mobilize at least $200 billion annually for biodiversity by 2030. Yet the United Nations Environment Program estimates that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, approximately 30 dollars go toward activities that harm it.
"We cannot close the biodiversity finance gap simply by adding more money while continuing to finance biodiversity destruction," Schomaker said.
COP17 needs to make progress in delivering financial commitments, improving access to funding, strengthening capacity and reforming harmful subsidies and incentives so that economic decisions support rather than undermine nature, she said.

paragraphs.en: At China's Xichang Satellite Launch Center, Ma Zhongquan has spent more than 20 years on Niutou Mountain, {{0}} the country's space program advance while building a career defined by {{1}} and growth. As a rocket blasts off, Ma and his colleagues keep their eyes fixed on their screens on Niutou Mountain, just a few kilometers away. Their job is to track the rocket from the very first moments of its flight. They also operate a {{2}} safety control system, ready to respond if a rocket {{3}} a {{4}} to the launch site or areas along its flight path. “Knowing that we are here gives our launch team peace of mind.

At China's Xichang Satellite Launch Center, Ma Zhongquan has spent more than 20 years on Niutou Mountain, witnessing the country's space program advance while building a career defined by dedication and growth.
As a rocket blasts off, Ma and his colleagues keep their eyes fixed on their screens on Niutou Mountain, just a few kilometers away. Their job is to track the rocket from the very first moments of its flight.
They also operate a specialized safety control system, ready to respond if a rocket poses a threat to the launch site or areas along its flight path.
“Knowing that we are here gives our launch team peace of mind. We describe ourselves as a sword that is always ready, but never drawn,” Ma said.
As a teenager, Ma watched a rocket launch with his father. The moment left a deep impression on him. He began to understand how closely a country's technological progress was connected to the hopes of ordinary people.
“My father had been so excited, but suddenly he became very quiet. That was the first time I realized that the country wasn't so far removed from our own family,” he recalled.
In 2003, Ma volunteered for a post at the Xichang Satellite Launch Center, taking on work in a remote mountain location where even access to drinking water was a challenge. He stayed on, witnessing two decades of technological change as equipment evolved from analog systems to automated tracking and data transmission.
“I've witnessed step by step how China's space program has grown stronger. I've taken part in missions involving BeiDou, lunar exploration and Mars exploration. I've been part of that journey,” Ma said.
Beyond his work at the launch center, Ma also visits schools to share the story of China's space program with the next generation.
“I hope to plant a seed of interest in space in every child's heart. Who knows? One day, it might take root and grow, just as it did for me,” he said.
But years of dedication on the mountain have also meant missing precious moments with his family. Asked whether a particular moment had stayed with him over the years, Ma recalled a difficult time when his family needed him.
“My wife called to tell me our child had a fever. She wanted me to come home and help, but I really couldn't leave because the mission was underway,” he said.
It was a difficult reminder that the demands of a mission can reach deep into family life.
In 2007, China successfully launched Chang'e-1, its first lunar probe. The achievement also brought Ma a personal message of encouragement from his former primary school teacher.
“My primary school teacher called and said, ‘I'm proud of you.’ I used to think that serving the country through aerospace was just a slogan. But at that moment, those words took on real weight,” Ma said.
Ma has also begun documenting the stories of those who have worked on Niutou Mountain. A poem he wrote about the mountain has also been engraved on its wall.
“I want future generations to know that a group of people on this mountain devoted themselves to their work and achieved something extraordinary,” he said.
In his spare time, Ma picks up his colored pencils to sketch the launch center and the mountain across the changing seasons. Over the years, he has captured not just the mountain's changing landscape, but also his deep connection to it.
Looking back on his journey, Ma was asked what his generation of aerospace workers had been protecting and what mission they would carry forward.
“China's space program is itself a Long March toward the universe. The older generation took us from zero to one and laid the foundation for us. The spirit of perseverance, truth-seeking and innovation at Xichang is also part of this Long March,” he said.
For more than 20 years, the technology has changed. China's space program has reached farther. Through every mission and every story he records, Ma continues his own journey. For him, the Long March of China's space program is also the Long March of his life.

我们把自己比作一把始终备而不出的剑，”马忠全说。少年时，马忠全曾和父亲一起观看火箭发射。那一刻给他留下了深刻印象。他开始明白，一个国家的技术进步与普通人的希望是多么紧密相连。“父亲当时非常激动，但突然变得非常安静。

那是我第一次意识到，国家离我们自己的家庭并不遥远，”他回忆道。2003年，马忠全主动申请到西昌卫星发射中心的一个岗位，在连饮用水都成问题的偏远山区工作。他留了下来，见证了二十年间的技术变迁，设备从模拟系统演进为自动化跟踪与数据传输。“我一步步见证了中国航天事业如何发展壮大。我参与了北斗、探月、火星探测等任务。

我是这段历程的一部分，”马忠全说。除了在发射中心的工作，马忠全还走进学校，向下一代讲述中国航天事业的故事。“我希望在每个孩子心中种下一颗对太空感兴趣的种子。谁知道呢？也许有一天它会生根发芽，就像当年在我心中那样，”他说。

2007年，中国成功发射首个月球探测器嫦娥一号。这一成就也为马忠全带来了小学老师发来的个人鼓励。“我的小学老师打电话说：‘我为你感到骄傲。’我曾以为航天报国只是一句口号。但那一刻，这些话有了真正的分量，”马忠全说。马忠全也开始记录那些曾在牛头山工作过的人们的故事。

Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Sunday's snap parliamentary election, as independent projections and leaders of a student-backed movement born out of anti-corruption protests confirmed an outright parliamentary majority that ends the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year grip on power.
Initial projections released by polling agencies Ipsos and CeSID showed the "Student List – Students Win" winning 52% of the vote, well ahead of Vucic's SNS-led coalition, "Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia," which stood at 39.3%.
Speaking at his campaign headquarters in Belgrade before final official results were available, Vucic said a stratified sample indicated that the student-backed list would win between 135 and 140 of the 250 parliamentary seats, compared with around 105 for his coalition.
"I want to inform you that based on the stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost these elections," Vucic said. "The student-backed list has won. They will have between 135 and 140 seats, and we will have around 105."
According to Vucic's projections, the student-backed list received approximately 2.2 million votes, while his coalition secured roughly 1.72 million.
Aleksandar Vucic, leader of the right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) speaks at the party headquarters, after conceding defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia, October 25, 2026. 
As victory celebrations erupted at the Student List's headquarters, prominent candidate Radomir Saicic, a University of Belgrade professor and member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, declared a historic triumph for Serbian citizens.
Stressing that the electoral will of the public "must be respected without exception," Saicic called on supporters to celebrate peacefully and with dignity, urging citizens not to fall for provocations or enter into conflicts.
Sunday's vote determined all 250 seats in Serbia's unicameral parliament, with 126 needed for a majority.
About 6.45 million voters were eligible to cast ballots at 8,392 polling stations, with 18 electoral lists competing. Polling stations closed at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT), though voters already in line at that hour were permitted to cast their ballots.
The outcome marks a major shift in Serbian politics, where Vucic and the SNS have held a dominant position since 2012. Vucic resigned as president on September 27 to take part in the parliamentary election, with a new presidential vote required by the end of December.
The student-backed movement emerged from nearly two years of anti-corruption protests and university blockades following the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. The tragedy became a focal point for public anger over corruption and demands for accountability.
The movement's electoral list, formally headed by Novi Sad university professor Ilija Srdanovic, campaigned on institutional reform and anti-corruption measures. It challenged not only the ruling bloc but also established opposition parties, including the Socialist Party of Serbia and other pro-European and right-wing groups.
In his concession address, Vucic said he had chosen to announce the projections before official results were released to spare supporters uncertainty and counter claims that he would refuse to acknowledge an electoral defeat.
He attributed his bloc's projected defeat to foreign support for the protest movement, describing the result as a "verification of a revolution."
Vucic thanked his supporters and pledged that his political movement would remain united and continue its work from the opposition benches.
The projections represent the most significant electoral setback for the SNS since it came to power in 2012 and place the student-backed movement in a position to form a single-party parliamentary majority.
